findings.finding: Generalise when moving a coefficient inside negatively powered brackets leaves the expression unchanged.
findings.breakdown: The task extends the coefficient-scope distinction explored in p6-q5.
findings.checked: For nonzero c and x, equality reduces to c^(n+1)=1. Over the reals, c=1 always works; c=-1 also works precisely when n is odd. This can be explained using reciprocal rules, repeated multiplication and parity.
findings.assumptions: n is a positive integer; c and x are nonzero real numbers.

repair.proposal: After p6-q5, offer: 'For a positive integer n, which nonzero real values of c make cx^(-n)=(cx)^(-n) for every nonzero x? Explain using positive and negative values of c.' Expected answer: c=1 for every n; c=-1 also works when n is odd. Cancelling x^(-n) gives c^(n+1)=1; a positive c other than 1 has a power different from 1, and a negative c must have magnitude 1 and an even exponent n+1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task includes the nonzero real domain and the parity-dependent answer.

findings.finding: p8-q2-v repeats the whole task in p7-practice-e without an explicit instructional purpose.
findings.breakdown: Both require expressing 7/(x^(-4)y^3) using positive indices, with identical values, factors and givens.
findings.checked: Compared both complete tasks and their enclosing prompts. Neither supplies a retrieval or comparison purpose; there are no differing parts or diagrams.
findings.assumptions: The supplied order is the intended booklet sequence.

repair.proposal: Remove p8-q2-v and retain p7-practice-e. Keep the distinct neighbouring p8-q2-w.

findings.finding: Compare which denominator factors move when the placement of negative indices changes.
findings.breakdown: The sequence isolates the distinction between a negatively powered factor and its neighbouring coefficient.
findings.checked: All proposed conversions are correct for nonzero variables. Each successive item changes the sign of one factor's index. Existing p8-q2 practice varies several features rather than providing this fixed-factor comparison.
findings.assumptions: x, a and b are nonzero.

repair.proposal: Between p8-q1 and p8-q2, ask: 'Before simplifying each expression, predict which factors will remain in the denominator.' Use 1/(3x^2), 1/(3x^(-2)), 1/(3^(-1)x^(-2)), 1/(3^(-1)x^2). Expected answers: 1/(3x^2), x^2/3, 3x^2, 3/x^2. The factors and index magnitudes stay fixed; one index sign changes at each step. Follow with the unpatterned item 5/(2a^(-3)b^2), giving 5a^3/(2b^2).

findings.doneWhen: The optional sequence includes predictions, the four controlled variations and the unpatterned follow-up.

findings.finding: The reciprocal topic does not rehearse the positive quotient-power rule used directly in its second worked example.
findings.breakdown: Following (y/x)^3=y^3/x^3 requires recalling that an outer power applies to both numerator and denominator. A student who recalls inversion alone may power only one entry.
findings.checked: Searched all supplied teaching and the immediately preceding denominator exercise. Neither provides a review of positive quotient powers. p6-q5 addresses a powered product, while p9-law-block states the combined rule without rehearsing this prior component.
findings.assumptions: Positive quotient powers are prior knowledge from the separate Index Laws course content. These symbolic review items do not require a calculator.

repair.proposal: Before p9-law-block, add: 'Write without brackets: (a/b)^2; (x/y)^3; (2/t)^2.' Expected answers: a^2/b^2; x^3/y^3; 4/t^2. Denominators are nonzero.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse applying a positive outer power to both entries of a quotient before p9-example-right-item.

findings.finding: Explain why reciprocal bases raised to the same negative integer power produce reciprocal results.
findings.breakdown: This generalises the existing adjacent comparison in p10-q1-i and p10-q1-j.
findings.checked: For nonzero a and b, the expressions become b^n/a^n and a^n/b^n, whose product is 1. The reciprocal and quotient-power methods are explicitly available in p9 teaching.
findings.assumptions: a and b are nonzero; n is a positive integer.

repair.proposal: After p10-q1-j, offer: 'The answers to (2/3)^(-2) and (3/2)^(-2) are reciprocals. Explain why (a/b)^(-n) and (b/a)^(-n) give reciprocal results for every positive integer n, when a and b are nonzero.' Expected answer: they equal b^n/a^n and a^n/b^n, so their product is 1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task retains the existing adjacent comparison and asks students to explain the general relationship.

findings.finding: p11-q2-p jumps from separately practised operations to combining two powered products with a negative outer power and powered coefficients.
findings.breakdown: Students must distribute two outer powers, reciprocate a coefficient, multiply signed indices and combine corresponding factors. No preceding item combines these demands; p11-q2-o is a routine single-variable quotient.
findings.checked: p6-q5 models one positively powered product; p9-guided-e-node handles one negatively powered quotient; p11-q2-e and f handle single powered products. These supply individual methods but do not bridge their simultaneous coordination. Although p concludes the exercise's harder closing run, the preceding routine items do not build towards that combined demand. Later p14-q11-a and p14-q12-a supply simpler combinations.
findings.assumptions: Students know positive-index laws and signed arithmetic. Calculator availability does not affect the identified coordination demand.

repair.proposal: Move p14-q11-a and then p14-q12-a immediately before p11-q2-p, removing their original occurrences. Retain their prompts: (a^3b^2)^3 × (a^2b^4)^(-1), followed by (3a^2b^(-2))^3 × (2a^4)^(-2). The first introduces combining two powered products with unit coefficients; the second adds powered numerical coefficients and a negative outer power of magnitude greater than one.

findings.doneWhen: Students encounter the two existing intermediate combinations before p11-q2-p, without duplicating them.

findings.finding: Generalise evaluation from a known fourth power to positive and negative multiples of four.
findings.breakdown: The task connects p13-q10's power-of-a-power reasoning with the booklet's reciprocal law.
findings.checked: x^4=3 guarantees x is nonzero. Consequently x^12=27, x^(-8)=1/9 and x^(4n)=3^n for every integer n, including zero. No choice between the possible real values of x is needed.
findings.assumptions: x is real and satisfies x^4=3; n is an integer.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p13-q10, offer: 'If x^4=3, find x^12 and x^(-8) without finding x. Then write a rule for x^(4n), where n is any integer, and explain why it works for negative n.' Expected answers: 27, 1/9 and x^(4n)=3^n. For n=-k with k positive, x^(-4k)=1/(x^4)^k=1/3^k; for n=0, the value is 1.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task includes the general rule and explanations for negative and zero indices.
